briefing: Israelis are voting at the fastest early pace in decades, with exit polls due around 4 p.m. Toronto time, while Reuters reports Washington and Ottawa are working on a deal to ease U.S. tariffs on Canadian steel and autos, possibly before the November 3 midterms. Queen's Park sits again today with student-aid spending under scrutiny, and the Bank of Canada is widely expected to raise rates on Wednesday as oil stays near US$115.
headline: Israel turnout runs high as U.S. and Canada eye tariff relief

stories.backstory: This is Israel's first national election since the Hamas attack of October 7, 2023, and the long Gaza war that followed. Netanyahu, the country's longest-serving prime minister, leads a coalition of Likud with ultra-Orthodox and far-right parties and is still on trial for corruption, which he denies. The opposition has campaigned on accountability for the security failures before October 7, while the war with Iran and the military-service exemption for ultra-Orthodox men are also major issues. In Israel the biggest party does not automatically govern; whoever can assemble 61 seats forms the government.
stories.headline: Israeli turnout hits early-hour high in vote seen as Netanyahu referendum
stories.impact: For Ontario residents the main channel is energy: a government seen as more or less willing to strike Iran again could move crude and gasoline prices at GTA pumps. The vote also matters to many Jewish, Arab and Muslim families in the GTA with ties to the region.
stories.now: Israel's Central Elections Committee put turnout at 16.7% by 10 a.m. (4 a.m. in Toronto), about 1.2 million votes, up from 15.9% at the same point in 2022. Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party filed an urgent complaint alleging ballot slips were being removed or defaced in areas that back him, and other parties reported similar problems; police separately arrested three men in the south over an alleged scheme to buy votes for the Arab party Ra'am. Polls close at 10 p.m. local time (4 p.m. in Toronto), when exit polls are released; final surveys showed the opposition at 52 to 54 of 120 Knesset seats and Netanyahu's coalition near 50, so neither side was close to the 61 needed. More than 7.3 million people are eligible to vote, and coalition talks could take weeks.

stories.backstory: The U.S. Supreme Court struck down Trump's broad emergency tariffs in February, but sector tariffs on steel, aluminum, autos, copper and lumber stayed. At the first CUSMA review on July 1, the U.S. refused to extend the deal for a full new term, so it now needs annual reviews. Ottawa walked out of talks on August 21, calling Washington's last-minute demands unfair. The U.S. imposed 50% tariffs on August 22, and Canada matched with counter-tariffs on September 8, plus a $25B support package for affected workers and businesses.
stories.headline: U.S. and Canada work on steel and auto tariff deal, possibly before midterms
stories.impact: Ontario manufacturers of flooring, carpets, paints and personal-care products face a 50% U.S. tariff from Friday, which could mean layoffs or reduced shifts. A real deal would matter most for GTA auto, steel and aluminum jobs, which are not yet covered by any relief.
stories.now: Citing two U.S. and four Canadian sources, Reuters says Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Canadian minister Dominic LeBlanc have been in regular contact on easing the Section 232 national-security tariffs: up to 50% on steel and 25% on autos. Canadian sources said a deal before the November 3 midterms is possible, though one industry source expects a narrow agreement if any; U.S. sources say Washington still wants more Canadian concessions, and Trump has said steel and auto tariffs rise to 50% on January 1, 2027 without a deal. Prime Minister Mark Carney says talks have intensified slightly and the U.S. is moving toward Canada's position, but he will not accept the U.S. offer from August. Separately, a U.S. order on October 30 adds 50% tariffs on Canadian flooring, carpets, shampoos, soaps and cocoa products while dropping them on some farm and forestry goods; Canada's counter-tariffs on about C$27.6 billion of U.S. goods remain.

stories.backstory: The U.S. and Israel began striking Iran on February 28, 2026, in the middle of nuclear talks. The first wave killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei. Iran answered with missiles and drones on Israel, Gulf states and U.S. bases, and closed the Strait of Hormuz, the channel that roughly a fifth of the world's oil normally passes through. A peace memorandum signed in June briefly reopened shipping, but it fell apart in July when Iran started attacking commercial ships again to press its claim over the strait.
stories.headline: Oil eases on Tehran talks but Brent stays near US$115
stories.impact: This is a big part of why gas and diesel in Ontario stay expensive: GTA regular is forecast around $1.80 a litre on Friday and diesel near $2.65. Diesel feeds straight into grocery and delivery prices, and higher fuel is one reason the Bank of Canada has been cautious about cutting rates.
stories.now: Saudi Defence Minister Khalid bin Salman, Pakistan's army chief Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin met Iranian leaders in Tehran on Monday and agreed to continue talks, though no concrete outcome was announced. Early Tuesday, Brent was down about US$1 at US$114.81 and U.S. crude (WTI) at about US$100.88; Brent topped US$117 last week after Iranian attacks on tankers near the Strait of Hormuz. Analysts say October has been the worst month on record for attacks on commercial shipping in and around the strait, and Gulf crude exports have fallen four weeks in a row. A U.S. intelligence memo says Iranian plots against Americans are at advanced stages, the State Department has cut embassy staff in Saudi Arabia, and Trump says he is weighing a deal or new strikes; Iran says it would reopen the strait if the U.S. lifts its naval blockade.

stories.backstory: Chow first won a 2023 by-election with 37% after John Tory resigned, and this was her first run as an incumbent. Bradford, a Beaches-East York councillor, ran on a first-year property-tax freeze and scrapping Toronto's land transfer tax on homes under $1.1 million, while Chow promised cheaper groceries, school lunches and more affordable housing. Mississauga's race pitted Parrish, elected in a 2024 by-election, against Crombie, who returned after leading the Ontario Liberals. All Ontario municipalities voted on the same day for four-year terms.
stories.headline: Chow re-elected; GTA voters oust mayors in Mississauga, Hamilton, Oakville and Milton
stories.impact: Toronto homeowners should expect Chow's budget approach to continue rather than Bradford's proposed tax freeze, and Mississauga residents can watch for Tedjo's promised two-year freeze on the residential tax levy. Ward councillor and school trustee results are posted on each city's website.
stories.now: Chow finished with about 54% to Brad Bradford's 41%, a lead of well over 100,000 votes, after polls had suggested a close race. Alvin Tedjo unseated Carolyn Parrish in Mississauga, and in Hamilton Keanin Loomis won with about 41% while Andrea Horwath fell to third at 14%. In Halton, Jeff Knoll took Oakville with 36% over incumbent Rob Burton, and George Minakakis beat Milton's long-time mayor Gord Krantz 45% to about 25%; Christina Early won Caledon with 59%. Patrick Brown (Brampton, 55%), Steven Del Duca (Vaughan, 81.5%), Frank Scarpitti (Markham, 71%) and David West (Richmond Hill, 83.5%) were re-elected, while Georgina, Oshawa and Clarington also chose new mayors.

stories.backstory: Oil prices jumped after the U.S.-Iran war closed much of the Strait of Hormuz earlier this year, and fuel costs have fed through to inflation since. Brent fell to about $74 in late June when shipping recovered, then climbed again as attacks resumed this autumn. Canada's central bank has weighed whether an energy-driven spike is temporary or will spread to other prices.
stories.headline: Retail sales rebound as markets bet on a Bank of Canada hike
stories.impact: Variable-rate mortgages and lines of credit would cost more within days of a hike, and anyone renewing a GTA mortgage this fall should test their budget at a higher rate. High pump prices will keep squeezing commuters either way.
stories.now: Statistics Canada's Friday report showed retail sales up about 1.2% in August, slightly below the 1.3% economists expected, with sales excluding autos also up 1.2%; that follows a 0.7% drop in July, and the agency's early estimate points to another 0.7% gain in September. Earlier this week, September inflation came in at 3.1%, driven by a 27.8% jump in gasoline prices, though inflation excluding gasoline was only 2.2% and the bank's core measures averaged about 1.9%. Swap markets have priced roughly an 80% or higher chance of a quarter-point hike to 2.50% next Wednesday, and BMO, RBC, Desjardins and Scotiabank now call for one. Arguing against a hike, Canada lost 68,000 jobs in September and unemployment rose to 6.5%. The loonie is holding near 71 U.S. cents, close to a four-week high. Friday's oil jump above US$116 adds to the pressure on gasoline prices.

stories.backstory: The spring 2026 budget pushed Ontario's target for balancing the books back to 2028-29. U.S. tariffs of up to 50% on Canadian goods have hit the province's steel, auto and lumber industries hardest. Fall economic statements update the budget's numbers and often add targeted tax or spending changes. This week Ottawa and Ontario announced an $8.7-billion plan for steel, autos and Ring of Fire roads.
stories.headline: Queen's Park returns today after 147 days, OSAP spending in focus
stories.impact: Students at private career colleges face an OSAP freeze until 2027, and any spending restraint in Thursday's update could reach health, education and transit services across the GTA.
stories.now: The legislature returns after a 147-day break for a short session of about 23 sitting days, and the Ontario Student Assistance Program (OSAP) is expected to dominate question period. Seven private career colleges received $385 million in OSAP grants in 2024-25, the same amount that went to all of Ontario's public colleges; Colleges Minister Nolan Quinn cut six schools from OSAP in May, ordered a KPMG audit in August and has referred the findings to the Ontario Provincial Police. The province has paused OSAP payments to career-college students for several months while it investigates. Bethlenfalvy tables the fall economic statement Thursday, with the deficit expected near the spring budget's $13.8-billion forecast, and the opposition plans to press on affordability and health care.

stories.backstory: Republicans have controlled both the House and Senate since January 2025, which has let Trump pass his agenda with few checks. Midterms usually go against the president's party, and Trump's approval is lower than at the same point in his first term. All 435 House seats and 35 Senate seats are on the ballot. A Democratic House could launch investigations and block spending and trade legislation.
stories.headline: Trump rallies in Mississippi as early vote tops 27 million
stories.impact: A change in Congress could shift the odds of tariff relief for Ontario's auto, steel and lumber industries. Ottawa's trade strategy is partly being timed around the outcome.
stories.now: In Corinth on Monday night, Trump spoke for more than 80 minutes for Hyde-Smith, who faces Democratic district attorney Scott Colom; he said he came because he can't take a chance and acknowledged Republicans could have a rough election night. Earlier Monday he offered $1 million on Truth Social for tips leading to election-fraud convictions. More than 27.4 million Americans had voted early as of Monday, including over 4.35 million in Texas. A federal appeals court ruled Trump broke federal law by taking control of California's National Guard for Los Angeles. Republicans hold the Senate 53–47, and the Cook Political Report estimates Democrats will gain 12 to 22 House seats.

stories.backstory: Russia's full-scale invasion is in its fifth year. Trump's envoys have made several trips to Moscow, while Zelenskyy has pushed for a leaders' meeting that Russia rejects. Russia has been pounding Ukraine's power grid ahead of winter, and Kyiv has struck Russian refineries in return. Ukraine has also complained about U.S. limits on intelligence sharing and a Starlink slowdown.
stories.headline: Oleshky truce holds locally as strikes continue elsewhere
stories.impact: Canada is a major Ukraine backer and is being asked for more money at the October 29–30 Canada-EU summit, which affects federal spending. Any real progress toward peace could ease diesel and gas prices over time.
stories.now: Russia's Defence Ministry says it halted shelling toward Kherson as the pause around Oleshky began, and Ukraine's negotiator Dmytro Lubinets says Kyiv is honouring it so food, medicine and evacuations can reach the town. Elsewhere, a Russian missile attack on Kyiv killed at least one person and injured 15, including students in a dormitory, and overnight strikes also hit Kharkiv and Pavlohrad. Russia says it intercepted 222 Ukrainian drones overnight; drone strikes killed two people in Russia's Bryansk region, and Russian-installed officials in occupied Zaporizhzhia say a drone hit a bus, killing one and injuring 30. No end date or outside monitor for the Oleshky truce has been announced.

stories.backstory: Tech giants have poured hundreds of billions of dollars into data centres and chips for AI, and those stocks have driven much of the market's gains. Investors have swung between excitement and doubt about whether the spending will pay off. This year's oil shock from the Iran war has also kept inflation and interest-rate worries alive.
stories.headline: Stocks close higher as Anthropic IPO filing revives the AI trade
stories.impact: Many Ontario RRSPs, TFSAs and pension plans hold U.S. tech through index funds, so today's bounce partly offsets last week's dip. A slightly weaker loonie makes cross-border shopping and U.S. trips a touch pricier.
stories.now: The S&P 500 finished Monday up 53.09 points, or 0.7%, at 7,676.77; the Dow rose 146.42 points to 52,361.58 and the Nasdaq climbed 214.04 points, or 0.8%, to 26,169.38. In Toronto the S&P/TSX composite closed up 0.44%, led by Hammond Power Solutions and CAE, while Celestica fell 4.8%. AI developer Anthropic publicly filed its S-1 prospectus (the registration document for an initial public offering) to list on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT, reporting US$16.3 billion of revenue in the first half of 2026, and Meta plans to raise US$35 billion by selling stock. Brent crude settled about 0.5% lower at US$110.21 a barrel and U.S. crude at US$101.33. Alphabet and Microsoft report Wednesday, the same day the Fed and the Bank of Canada announce rate decisions.

stories.backstory: Cleveland-Cliffs, an Ohio steelmaker, bought Hamilton-based Stelco in 2024, and Ottawa approved the deal on condition that union jobs and most non-union roles be kept. U.S. 50% tariffs on Canadian steel since August have hit exports hard. In early October Stelco announced a partial shutdown of finishing lines at Hamilton Works, cutting up to 500 jobs, and Joly gave the company five days to respond. The dispute has become a test of whether Ottawa can enforce foreign-takeover promises.
stories.headline: Ottawa gives Stelco owner 15 days to reverse layoffs
stories.impact: Hundreds of Hamilton families face lost paycheques, with knock-on effects for suppliers and the local economy. The outcome may shape whether the new federal-Ontario steel fund keeps similar plants running.
stories.now: In a letter sent Thursday, Joly gave Cleveland-Cliffs 15 days to meet the job commitments it made when it bought Stelco in 2024, or face court action. She says Ottawa has found a breach and that a forced sale is on the table, adding that some potential buyers have shown interest. Up to 500 jobs at the Hamilton and Lake Erie operations are affected, and about 200 workers have already been laid off. Cleveland-Cliffs, which blames 50% U.S. tariffs and low steel prices, has not commented on the letter, while Premier Doug Ford and the steelworkers' union back Ottawa.

stories.backstory: Since U.S. tariffs hit Canadian steel, aluminum, autos and lumber, Carney has pushed to sell more to other markets. Canada and the EU already trade under the CETA free-trade deal, and in February 2026 Canada became the first non-European country to join the EU's SAFE defence-procurement program. Ottawa has also been courting Gulf investors and, separately, is racing to finish a trade deal with India before Modi's December visit.
stories.headline: Carney and premiers open first meeting with First Nations in 20 years
stories.impact: Projects such as Ontario's Ring of Fire mining region depend on First Nations agreements, which affects future jobs and investment in the province. Few immediate effects for GTA households.
stories.now: Carney opened the Ottawa meeting saying it will help build new relationships as his government pursues a major-projects building boom; it is the first in-person meeting of first ministers with First Nations leaders in about 20 years, and the premiers of Alberta, B.C. and Quebec are not attending. Assembly of First Nations National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak said First Nations fought hard for the meeting and it should not be the last. Many chiefs worry Bill C-39, the Building Canada Strong Act and its 'one project, one review, one year' approach, could sidestep the duty to consult, which Crown-Indigenous Relations Minister Rebecca Alty says stays in place. Abu Dhabi's Crown Prince also visits October 26–27, and Carney hosts EU leaders in Montreal on October 29–30.

stories.backstory: Peltola, a former one-term congresswoman, topped the August nonpartisan primary and is in a close race with Sullivan. Alaska uses ranked-choice voting, so voters can rank both Sullivans if they are unsure. Democrats and voting-rights groups have long warned the administration might try to stop states from certifying races Trump's party loses. Under the Constitution, states run their own elections within rules set by Congress.
stories.headline: Justice Department sues to block a possible Democratic win in Alaska
stories.impact: There is no direct effect on Ontario, but a fight over who controls the U.S. Senate would shape how much room Trump has on tariffs against Canada next year.
stories.now: The U.S. Justice Department filed the suit in federal court in Alaska, 11 days before the November 3 vote, and Trump said he ordered it. It targets Daniel J. Sullivan of Petersburg, who appears on the ballot with no party label and drew 4,107 votes (about 2%) in the August primary, versus more than 68,000 for the incumbent. The suit also asks for a probe into whether votes for him were meant for the senator; Republicans call him a Democratic plant, which he denies, and Alaska's Supreme Court already refused to remove him. Attorney General Todd Blanche said the department does not aim to interfere improperly, while Democrats called it a sham, and a Notre Dame election-law expert said the statute does not appear to allow blocking certification. Separately, Fox News reports Peltola and family members suffered minor injuries in a two-vehicle crash in Anchorage on Saturday night, and her campaign postponed some appearances.

stories.backstory: Eby's NDP won a one-seat majority in October 2024, just ahead of a Conservative party that had surged from almost nowhere. On September 22, 2026, Eby called an election two years early, while the Conservatives had only just chosen a new leader, which critics said was unfair. Days before the call, eight Conservative members had broken away to form a new party, CentreBC, though seven later returned. Lorne Doerkson now leads the Conservatives, and Emily Lowan leads the Greens.
stories.headline: B.C.'s Doerkson says voters 'chose change,' names transition team
stories.impact: Little changes day to day in Ontario, but a B.C. government keen on more LNG and pipelines could strengthen Ottawa's push for energy exports that bypass the U.S. It also adds another premier at the table on trade and federal transfers that affect Ontario.
stories.now: Doerkson said he was humbled by the win, named former deputy minister Kim Henderson to lead the transition, and promised an independent review of B.C.'s finances on day one and an expert panel on emergency-room closures within 100 days. His first priority is raising the basic personal income-tax exemption to $32,000, which he says saves workers about $1,000 a year; no swearing-in date is set and he did not rule out a fall sitting. Unofficial results give the Conservatives 64 seats (about 48% of the vote), the NDP 27 (37%) and the Greens 2 (11%), on a preliminary turnout of about 48%, the lowest in decades. Doerkson, technically an interim leader, said he will stay on and called that an administrative detail; he repeated plans to repeal B.C.'s Indigenous rights law, known as DRIPA. David Eby has resigned as NDP leader, and mail-in ballots are added at the final count on November 6 to 10.

stories.why: B.C. joins Alberta, Saskatchewan and Ontario with right-of-centre premiers, shifting the balance as Ottawa negotiates with Washington and pushes pipelines and major projects. Doerkson's LNG and carbon-tax plans could reopen national energy and climate debates.

stories.backstory: Lula, a leftist, returned to power in 2023 after narrowly beating Jair Bolsonaro in 2022. Jair Bolsonaro was barred from office and later convicted over a coup plot, so his son Flávio became the right's candidate. Flávio led the October 4 first round by about 2 points and most final polls showed a tie or a slim Bolsonaro edge. The campaign centred on crime, taxes, the cost of living and relations with Trump's Washington, which had hoped for a Bolsonaro win.
stories.headline: Brazil's real plunges as Bolsonaro seeks to annul Lula's runoff win
stories.impact: Little direct effect on daily life in the GTA, but Canadian pension funds and mining, energy and bank investors with Brazilian holdings are taking a hit from today's selloff. A Lula government remains a potential partner for Canada's trade diversification away from the U.S.
stories.now: São Paulo's Bovespa index was down about 14.6% Monday afternoon after Lula's win surprised investors who had bet on Flávio Bolsonaro, and the real fell more than 8% against the U.S. dollar at the open, which El País called its steepest drop since 1999. Lula took 51.79% of the vote, according to the electoral court, a margin of nearly 4.4 million votes on turnout of about 81%. Bolsonaro has not conceded and is seeking to annul the result, calling the two-hour voting extension inexplicable, although both campaigns had asked for it. Lula, 80, begins his new term on January 5, 2027.

stories.summary: Markets that had bet on Flávio Bolsonaro sold off hard Monday after Lula won Sunday's runoff with about 51.8%, while Bolsonaro refuses to concede.

timeline.event: Lula narrowly beats Jair Bolsonaro.
First round: Flávio Bolsonaro leads Lula 47% to 45%.
Final polls show a statistical tie.
Voting extended two hours; count paused, then resumed.
TSE declares Lula the winner with 51.8%.
Real falls 8%+, stock futures hit limit down.

stories.why: Brazil is Latin America's largest economy and a top exporter of food and commodities. Lula's win keeps a government that has resisted pressure from the Trump administration, and the result is a setback for Trump, who had backed the Bolsonaro camp.
